quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Stacked Relative Clauses
quests.questionSentence: The pilot who landed the aircraft that lost an engine over the Pacific received a medal. What does 'that lost an engine over the Pacific' describe?
quests.targetClause: the aircraft
quests.completedSentence: The pilot who landed the aircraft that lost an engine over the Pacific received a medal. What does 'that lost an engine over the Pacific' describe?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'That lost an engine over the Pacific' modifies 'the aircraft,' the noun directly before it. The earlier clause, 'who landed the aircraft,' modifies 'the pilot.' In stacked clauses, each relative word attaches to the nearest noun that makes sense with its verb.
quests.nativeTip: Two clauses are stacked here. Ask which noun sits directly in front of 'that' and whether it can logically be the thing that lost an engine.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "the aircraft"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Stacked Relative Clauses
quests.questionSentence: The scientist who discovered the enzyme ___ regulates blood sugar received a prestigious prize.
quests.targetClause: which
quests.completedSentence: The scientist who discovered the enzyme which regulates blood sugar received a prestigious prize.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The enzyme' is the antecedent of this blank, and it is the subject of 'regulates,' so a pronoun for things is needed: 'which.' The earlier 'who' already belongs to 'the scientist'; a personal pronoun cannot refer to an enzyme.
quests.nativeTip: Two clauses, two antecedents. This blank belongs to the second one, so ask which noun stands directly before it and what that noun is doing.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "which"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Possessive Relative Pronoun whose
quests.questionSentence: The farmer whose orchard the council wanted to buy refused to sell. What does 'whose' link together in this sentence?
quests.targetClause: The farmer and the orchard, because the farmer owns it
quests.completedSentence: The farmer whose orchard the council wanted to buy refused to sell. What does 'whose' link together in this sentence?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Whose' links 'the farmer' (the owner) to 'orchard' (the thing owned). The council is the subject of 'wanted to buy,' so it plays no part in the possession relationship.
quests.nativeTip: 'Whose' always connects an owner to the noun that comes right after it.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The farmer and the orchard, because the farmer owns it"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Defining vs Non-Defining Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: Our firm has three offices - Denver, Austin, and Portland - but only the Austin office handles international clients. Which sentence best reflects this?
quests.targetClause: The office that handles international clients is in Austin.
quests.completedSentence: Our firm has three offices - Denver, Austin, and Portland - but only the Austin office handles international clients. Which sentence best reflects this?
quests.ruleExplanation: With three offices, the clause is essential because it tells us which office is meant, so it is defining: no commas, and 'that' is fine. Commas would suggest the firm has only one office, and 'that' can never follow a comma.
quests.nativeTip: Decide whether the clause has to pick one office out of several, or just adds a fact about an office that is already identified.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The office that handles international clients is in Austin."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Comma Placement in Non-Defining Clauses
quests.questionSentence: A rural clinic has exactly one physician. She trained in Havana and speaks three languages. Which brochure sentence uses the Havana fact correctly?
quests.targetClause: The physician, who trained in Havana, speaks three languages.
quests.completedSentence: A rural clinic has exactly one physician. She trained in Havana and speaks three languages. Which brochure sentence uses the Havana fact correctly?
quests.ruleExplanation: Because there is only one physician, 'who trained in Havana' is non-defining: it needs a comma on each side and cannot use 'that.' Without commas, the sentence would suggest the clinic has several physicians and this is the one who trained in Havana.
quests.nativeTip: Only one physician exists, so the Havana detail is extra background. Check both the commas and the pronoun.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "The physician, who trained in Havana, speaks three languages."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Defining vs Non-Defining Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: A school newsletter says: 'Students who complete the survey will receive a free lunch coupon.' A parent argues that her daughter, who was absent on survey day, should receive one too. Does the sentence support her argument?
quests.targetClause: No - the clause has no commas, so it limits the coupons to students who completed the survey.
quests.completedSentence: A school newsletter says: 'Students who complete the survey will receive a free lunch coupon.' A parent argues that her daughter, who was absent on survey day, should receive one too. Does the sentence support her argument?
quests.ruleExplanation: The clause has no commas, so it is defining: it limits the coupons to the students who completed the survey. A parent cannot read the sentence as a promise to every student.
quests.nativeTip: Ask whether 'who complete the survey' narrows down a group or simply describes everyone in it.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "No - the clause has no commas, so it limits the coupons to students who completed the survey."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Where vs Which/That for Places
quests.questionSentence: The warehouse ___ the company leased in 2015 flooded during the storm.
quests.targetClause: that
quests.completedSentence: The warehouse that the company leased in 2015 flooded during the storm.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Leased' takes 'the warehouse' as its direct object, so an object relative pronoun ('that') is needed. 'Where' would only work if the warehouse were the location of some other action, and 'whom' is for people.
quests.nativeTip: 'The company leased' something - ask whether the warehouse is the thing being leased or merely the setting for an action.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "that"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Relative Adverb of Place (where)
quests.questionSentence: The warehouse ___ the company stores its winter inventory flooded during the storm.
quests.targetClause: where
quests.completedSentence: The warehouse where the company stores its winter inventory flooded during the storm.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Stores' already has its object, 'its winter inventory,' so the warehouse is only the place where the storing happens. 'Where' (meaning 'in which') fits; 'which' alone would leave the clause without the preposition it needs.
quests.nativeTip: 'Stores' already has its object - 'its winter inventory.' What job is left for the warehouse?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "where"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Relative Adverbs Cannot Be Subjects
quests.questionSentence: The storm ___ flooded the warehouse also closed the airport.
quests.targetClause: which
quests.completedSentence: The storm which flooded the warehouse also closed the airport.
quests.ruleExplanation: Nothing else performs 'flooded,' so the gap must supply the subject - a job only relative pronouns can do. 'When' and 'where' are adverbs and can never be subjects; 'which' refers back to the storm.
quests.nativeTip: Check whether 'flooded' has a subject anywhere else. If the gap must be the subject, can an adverb do that job?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "which"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Possessive Relative Pronoun whose
quests.questionSentence: The museum, ___ collection includes over 50,000 artifacts, reopens in June.
quests.targetClause: whose
quests.completedSentence: The museum, whose collection includes over 50,000 artifacts, reopens in June.
quests.ruleExplanation: The collection belongs to the museum, so the possessive 'whose' is needed. It works for things as well as people, and here it introduces a non-defining clause; 'that' could never follow a comma.
quests.nativeTip: Look at the noun right after the gap. What owns it? Also notice the commas around the clause.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "whose"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Possessive Relative Pronoun whose
quests.questionSentence: Which pair of sentences could be combined into one using 'whose'?
quests.targetClause: The band released an album. The band's tour sold out in a day.
quests.completedSentence: Which pair of sentences could be combined into one using 'whose'?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The band's tour' shows possession, so the pair becomes 'The band whose tour sold out in a day released an album.' In the other pairs the second sentence is about the album itself, which calls for 'that' or 'which' rather than 'whose.'
quests.nativeTip: 'Whose' replaces a possessive form (X's Y). Look for the pair where one noun owns or belongs to the other.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The band released an album. The band's tour sold out in a day."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Possessive Relative Pronoun whose
quests.questionSentence: The driver whose licence the officer confiscated appealed the decision. Inside the relative clause, what is the grammatical role of 'the officer'?
quests.targetClause: The subject of 'confiscated'
quests.completedSentence: The driver whose licence the officer confiscated appealed the decision. Inside the relative clause, what is the grammatical role of 'the officer'?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Whose licence' is the object of 'confiscated' - the officer took it. The officer performs the action, so 'the officer' is the subject. 'Whose' only supplies the possessive link back to 'the driver.'
quests.nativeTip: Find the verb 'confiscated' and ask who performed the confiscating.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The subject of 'confiscated'"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Whom in Formal Register
quests.questionSentence: Casual: 'The consultant we picked last year keeps missing deadlines.' Which is the most formal rewrite for a board report?
quests.targetClause: The consultant whom we selected last year has repeatedly missed deadlines.
quests.completedSentence: Casual: 'The consultant we picked last year keeps missing deadlines.' Which is the most formal rewrite for a board report?
quests.ruleExplanation: In a formal report, the omitted pronoun is restored, and because the consultant is the object of 'selected,' the formal choice is 'whom.' 'Which' cannot refer to a person, and the stray comma would wrongly turn the clause into extra information.
quests.nativeTip: Formal writing restores the pronoun and uses the traditional object form for a person.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The consultant whom we selected last year has repeatedly missed deadlines."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Non-Defining Clauses Cannot Omit Their Pronoun
quests.grammarRule: Non-Defining Clauses Cannot Omit Their Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: Formal: 'My supervisor, whom I greatly respect, retired last week.' Which casual version keeps the same meaning and is still grammatical?
quests.targetClause: My boss, who I really respect, retired last week.
quests.completedSentence: Formal: 'My supervisor, whom I greatly respect, retired last week.' Which casual version keeps the same meaning and is still grammatical?
quests.ruleExplanation: Casual English can swap 'whom' for 'who,' but this is a non-defining clause, so the pronoun and both commas must stay. Dropping the pronoun and commas would turn it into a defining clause suggesting several bosses, 'that' can never follow a comma, and the last option is missing its closing comma.
quests.nativeTip: Casual speech can relax 'whom,' but a clause set off by commas still needs a visible pronoun - and one particular pronoun is never allowed after a comma.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "My boss, who I really respect, retired last week."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Whom in Formal Register
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence would suit a formal news editorial AND is correctly punctuated, given that the town has only one mayor?
quests.targetClause: The mayor, whom voters elected by a narrow margin, faces a recall vote.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence would suit a formal news editorial AND is correctly punctuated, given that the town has only one mayor?
quests.ruleExplanation: Since there is one mayor, the clause is non-defining and needs commas on both sides. 'Whom' is the formal object pronoun for a person, matching an editorial's register. 'Who' is more casual, 'that' can never follow a comma, and dropping the commas would imply several mayors.
quests.nativeTip: Two tests at once: is the punctuation right for a unique mayor, and is the pronoun the formal choice for a person in object position?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "The mayor, whom voters elected by a narrow margin, faces a recall vote."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: That Cannot Introduce Non-Defining Clauses
quests.questionSentence: What is the error in this sentence? 'The festival, that draws visitors from across the country, begins in July.'
quests.targetClause: 'That' has been used to introduce a non-defining clause; 'which' is required.
quests.completedSentence: What is the error in this sentence? 'The festival, that draws visitors from across the country, begins in July.'
quests.ruleExplanation: The commas are appropriate, since the festival is unique and the clause adds extra information. The problem is 'that': it can never introduce a non-defining clause, so 'which' must replace it.
quests.nativeTip: Look at the punctuation first, then check which relative pronouns may follow a comma.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "'That' has been used to introduce a non-defining clause; 'which' is required."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted
quests.grammarRule: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted
quests.questionSentence: What is the error in this sentence? 'The applicant submitted the incomplete form was rejected.'
quests.targetClause: A subject relative pronoun has been dropped; 'who' or 'that' is needed before 'submitted.'
quests.completedSentence: What is the error in this sentence? 'The applicant submitted the incomplete form was rejected.'
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Submitted' has no subject of its own - 'the applicant' must supply it - so the subject relative pronoun ('who' or 'that') cannot be dropped. Only object relative pronouns in defining clauses can be omitted.
quests.nativeTip: Ask which noun is the subject of 'submitted' and whether anything else in the sentence could supply that subject.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "A subject relative pronoun has been dropped; 'who' or 'that' is needed before 'submitted.'"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: That Cannot Introduce Non-Defining Clauses
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence contains two separate errors - one with the pronoun and one with the punctuation?
quests.targetClause: The author, that wrote the memoir was invited to speak.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence contains two separate errors - one with the pronoun and one with the punctuation?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The author, that wrote the memoir was invited to speak' has two errors: 'that' cannot follow a comma, and the closing comma is missing. The defining and non-defining versions are both correct, and the sentence with only a stray comma has just one error.
quests.nativeTip: Count the problems in each sentence separately: pronoun choice and comma balance are different skills.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "The author, that wrote the memoir was invited to speak."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Defining vs Non-Defining Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: Policy A: 'Claims that involve water damage are excluded.' Policy B: 'Claims, which involve water damage, are excluded.' A customer files a claim for fire damage. Under which policy is her claim still covered?
quests.targetClause: Policy A only
quests.completedSentence: Policy A: 'Claims that involve water damage are excluded.' Policy B: 'Claims, which involve water damage, are excluded.' A customer files a claim for fire damage. Under which policy is her claim still covered?
quests.ruleExplanation: In Policy A the clause is defining: only claims involving water damage are excluded, so a fire claim survives. In Policy B the commas make the clause non-defining, describing all claims as water-related and excluding every one of them.
quests.nativeTip: Ask whether each clause narrows down which claims are excluded or describes all claims.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "Policy A only"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Defining vs Non-Defining Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: The staff handbook says: 'Employees, who work remotely, must attend the monthly meeting.' What does this sentence imply?
quests.targetClause: That every employee works remotely, so everyone must attend.
quests.completedSentence: The staff handbook says: 'Employees, who work remotely, must attend the monthly meeting.' What does this sentence imply?
quests.ruleExplanation: With commas, 'who work remotely' is non-defining: it adds a fact about all the employees rather than picking out a subset. To limit the rule to remote workers, the handbook would need to drop the commas.
quests.nativeTip: Commas turn the clause into extra information about a group that is already fully identified.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "That every employee works remotely, so everyone must attend."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Possessive Relative Pronoun whose
quests.questionSentence: An airline sign reads: 'Passengers, whose bags exceed 23 kg, must pay a fee.' Why is this version misleading?
quests.targetClause: The commas suggest that every passenger's bags exceed 23 kg.
quests.completedSentence: An airline sign reads: 'Passengers, whose bags exceed 23 kg, must pay a fee.' Why is this version misleading?
quests.ruleExplanation: The commas make the clause non-defining, so it seems to describe all passengers. The airline means only those with heavy bags, which requires no commas: 'Passengers whose bags exceed 23 kg must pay a fee.'
quests.nativeTip: Think about what commas do to a clause: do they select some passengers, or describe all of them?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "The commas suggest that every passenger's bags exceed 23 kg."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Antecedent Identification
quests.questionSentence: The report on urban air quality that the city commissioned last year, which relied on data from forty sensors, recommends stricter limits. What does 'which relied on data from forty sensors' describe?
quests.targetClause: the report
quests.completedSentence: The report on urban air quality that the city commissioned last year, which relied on data from forty sensors, recommends stricter limits. What does 'which relied on data from forty sensors' describe?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The report' - the one the city commissioned - relied on sensor data. 'Last year' is just a time phrase, and 'urban air quality' is what the report is about. The comma shows this clause adds extra detail.
quests.nativeTip: The nearest noun is 'last year,' but ask what could logically have relied on sensor data.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "the report"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Relative Clause Recognition
quests.questionSentence: In 'The startup whose founders dropped out of university and moved to Berlin raised forty million euros,' which words make up the relative clause?
quests.targetClause: whose founders dropped out of university and moved to Berlin
quests.completedSentence: In 'The startup whose founders dropped out of university and moved to Berlin raised forty million euros,' which words make up the relative clause?
quests.ruleExplanation: The relative clause starts at 'whose' and runs through 'Berlin.' The main verb 'raised' belongs to 'the startup' - the antecedent - so it falls outside the clause.
quests.nativeTip: A relative clause begins with the relative word and ends just before the main verb that belongs to the antecedent.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "whose founders dropped out of university and moved to Berlin"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Omission of Object Relative Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: Researchers who studied the effect ___ the drug had on memory reported mixed results.
quests.targetClause: (no word needed)
quests.completedSentence: Researchers who studied the effect (no word needed) the drug had on memory reported mixed results.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The drug' is the subject of 'had,' so 'the effect' is the object, and this defining clause can drop its pronoun. The first clause ('who studied') is a subject relative clause, so its pronoun must stay.
quests.nativeTip: Look at the second clause only. 'The drug' already has a job - 'had.' What does that leave for 'the effect'?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "(no word needed)"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Whom in Formal Register
quests.questionSentence: In the company's formal incident report, the analyst wrote: 'The technician of the regional office ___ the manufacturer eventually dispatched had never serviced that model.'
quests.targetClause: whom
quests.completedSentence: In the company's formal incident report, the analyst wrote: 'The technician of the regional office whom the manufacturer eventually dispatched had never serviced that model.'
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The manufacturer' is the subject of 'dispatched,' so 'the technician' is the object. In a formal report, the object pronoun for a person is 'whom.'
quests.nativeTip: The manufacturer dispatched someone. Ask who does the dispatching and who is dispatched, then consider the formal setting.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "whom"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Possessive Relative Pronoun whose
quests.questionSentence: The seminar on climate finance, ___ organizers received over three hundred applications, was cancelled at the last minute.
quests.targetClause: whose
quests.completedSentence: The seminar on climate finance, whose organizers received over three hundred applications, was cancelled at the last minute.
quests.ruleExplanation: The organizers belong to the seminar, so the possessive 'whose' is needed. 'Which' and 'who' cannot show possession, and 'that' can never appear in a clause set off by commas.
quests.nativeTip: Ask what belongs to the seminar, and notice the commas around the clause.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "whose"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Relative Adverb of Place (where)
quests.questionSentence: The cafe near the station ___ we met every Friday during college has finally closed.
quests.targetClause: where
quests.completedSentence: The cafe near the station where we met every Friday during college has finally closed.
quests.ruleExplanation: We met each other at the cafe; 'met' does not take the cafe as its object. The cafe is only the setting, so the relative adverb 'where' (meaning 'at which') is correct.
quests.nativeTip: Does 'met' take the cafe as its object, or does the cafe just provide the setting?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "where"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Defining vs Non-Defining Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: A company has one CEO and several regional directors. Which sentence is correct and reflects this?
quests.targetClause: The CEO, who founded the firm, promoted the director whom she trusted most.
quests.completedSentence: A company has one CEO and several regional directors. Which sentence is correct and reflects this?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Who founded the firm' is non-defining because there is only one CEO: it takes commas and cannot use 'that.' 'Whom she trusted most' is defining because it picks one director from several, so it takes no commas. The other options mismatch the punctuation to the situation.
quests.nativeTip: Check each clause against its own antecedent: one is unique, one is chosen from several.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "The CEO, who founded the firm, promoted the director whom she trusted most."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Omission of Object Relative Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: In 'The advice the mentor gave the student who struggled most helped everyone,' which statement about omitted pronouns is correct?
quests.targetClause: 'The mentor gave the student' modifies 'advice' and has lost 'that' or 'which.'
quests.completedSentence: In 'The advice the mentor gave the student who struggled most helped everyone,' which statement about omitted pronouns is correct?
quests.ruleExplanation: The mentor gave the advice, so the omitted object pronoun belongs to 'advice.' The clause 'who struggled most' is a subject relative clause and keeps its pronoun, as it must.
quests.nativeTip: Find the noun that the mentor actually gave, and check whether 'who struggled most' still has a visible pronoun.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "'The mentor gave the student' modifies 'advice' and has lost 'that' or 'which.'"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Relative Adverbs Cannot Be Subjects
quests.questionSentence: Which statement about relative clauses is FALSE?
quests.targetClause: Relative adverbs such as 'where' can serve as the subject of their clause.
quests.completedSentence: Which statement about relative clauses is FALSE?
quests.ruleExplanation: Relative adverbs (where, when, why) can never be the subject of their clause - only relative pronouns can. The other three statements are true: 'that' works in defining clauses for people and things, non-defining clauses keep their pronoun, and object pronouns in defining clauses can often be dropped.
quests.nativeTip: Test each statement against what you know about subjects, commas, and omission.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "Relative adverbs such as 'where' can serve as the subject of their clause."
